# Public release code review

This is a historical review of tracked TypeScript, browser JavaScript, fixtures, CLI commands, configuration and documentation. Later verification is recorded in [QA.md](QA.md); the current candidate and publication gates are in [RELEASE.md](RELEASE.md). This review does not claim that every possible defect is eliminated.

## Findings addressed

| Finding                                                                   | Change                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Node 20 declared despite Commander requiring Node 22                      | Runtime minimum aligned to 22.13; Node types match that baseline                                    |
| TypeScript 7 incompatible with current typescript-eslint peer range       | Supported TypeScript 6.0 selected without forcing peer dependencies                                 |
| Unformatted source and no automated quality gate                          | Prettier, ESLint, strict compiler checks, editor settings and CI                                    |
| Core imported CLI implementation; shared infrastructure lived in sync     | Launch/status services and focused errors, values, file-store, transactions, lock and shell modules |
| Import could leave credentials, registry and provenance partially updated | One interprocess lock, checked source/hub inputs and compensating rollback                          |
| Registry read errors could become an empty registry                       | Shared runtime schema and fail-closed configuration reads                                           |
| Dotenv parser lost multiline or escaped credentials                       | Preserving parser/writer with round-trip tests for quotes, escapes, newlines and Unicode            |
| Credentials inside URLs could remain in tracked registry                  | Extract credential-bearing URLs and arguments into `.env`; regression coverage                      |
| Import staged every hub file automatically                                | Import does not commit; initialization commits only its explicit setup files                        |
| Prototype-specific migration and takeover                                 | Removed implicit migration/ownership exceptions; normal reviewed import applies                     |
| Hardcoded n8n behavior in domain/UI                                       | Generic readiness configuration and generic UI labels, optional isolated preset                     |
| Copyable commands assumed a POSIX shell                                   | Central POSIX/PowerShell rendering with quoting tests                                               |
| DSH import and sync resolved profiles differently                         | Shared settings parser and profile resolver                                                         |
| Personal email/domain in design examples                                  | Replaced with example.com identities                                                                |
| UI runtime depended on design mockup assets                               | Self-contained runtime assets and package-content verification                                      |
| Duplicate fingerprint serialization and policies                          | Shared serialization and adapter-local policy definitions                                           |

The CLI and UI use the same domain services. Client-specific formats and platform opening/cleanup logic remain explicit integrations; those are necessary compatibility rules rather than user-specific assumptions. No user home, email, machine path or corporate host is compiled into the runtime.

## Validation baseline

The local quality gate covers formatting, lint, TypeScript, full integration/unit tests and package contents. Coverage reports include compiled runtime files, not fixture code. The local baseline is **54 passing tests**, **86.20% runtime lines**, **81.46% branches** and **84.68% functions**. The full CLI flow also runs from an unrelated working directory with all three client locations overridden. The complete suite also passed locally under Node **22.13.0**, the declared minimum. Later test runs are the authoritative result.

The production dependency audit reported **zero vulnerabilities**. The full development tree reported a moderate minimatch denial-of-service advisory propagated through ESLint tooling. The affected patterns are repository-controlled lint configuration, and those tools are excluded from the release runtime. No unsupported dependency override or forced downgrade was applied. Review upstream fixes before publishing; this advisory is not represented as resolved.

## Remaining limits

- macOS/Linux are supported targets. PowerShell command rendering is tested as text; Windows subprocess-tree cleanup, permissions and native client wrappers still need end-to-end verification. Windows is experimental.
- CI is configured for macOS/Linux and Node 22.13/24. Local macOS success does not establish remote CI success.
- File replacement is atomic per file and flushed before rename. Multi-file rollback cannot guarantee recovery after abrupt process or machine termination. External applications do not honor the hub lock; a narrow check-to-rename race remains.
- A crashed process can leave the lock file. Recovery is explicit after verifying that the owner has stopped; the application does not guess whether a reused PID is safe to ignore.
- Secret extraction uses conservative heuristics. Review imported definitions before tracking or sharing a hub. Already committed secrets require removal and rotation outside this tool.
- The dependency audit covers the lockfile, not user-configured executables or packages downloaded by external launchers.
- Readiness probes are optional unauthenticated HTTP checks. They do not execute tools or establish provider API permissions, and an ingress may obscure the actual service state.
- Interactive terminal prompts and desktop browser-opening behavior are not fully automated by the unit suite. Source-level browser helpers and HTTP boundaries are tested; this pass does not claim a full automated browser matrix.
- Instruction delivery and repository initialization are implemented. Chat capture and indexing are now available; see [HISTORY.md](HISTORY.md). Native session transfer remains separate.
- The candidate version is 0.1.0-beta.1, distributed as reviewed archives. Public npm registry publication remains deferred; this review did not publish a package.

## Follow-up: original-state recovery

A later audit added external baselines, a durable write-intent journal, `reset`, explicit stale-lock recovery and regression cases for interrupted sync/reset. See [EDGE_CASES.md](EDGE_CASES.md) and [RECOVERY.md](RECOVERY.md). These improve process-failure recovery; they do not establish database-style crash durability or remove the filesystem limits listed above.

# Historical research: alternatives and product direction

These notes summarize research collected on 2026-11-02. They are product-planning context, not a current feature comparison or a recommendation to install another tool. Repository capabilities, activity and popularity were not revalidated for this documentation update. The current Agent Hub contract is described in [Quick start](QUICKSTART.md) and [Design](DESIGN.md).

## Problems explored

The original research looked at several separate needs: sharing MCP definitions, distributing complete skills, keeping instructions consistent, carrying task state between agents, retaining useful knowledge, and searching old conversations. These needs overlap, but a tool that addresses one does not necessarily solve the others.

Agent Hub's direction is a local canonical store with reviewed client projections, visible conflicts, private credential references, and recoverable writes. Quick setup reduces the number of steps required to reach that result. It does not claim automatic interoperability with every native memory format or archived session.

## Projects considered

| Area                           | Examples in the original research                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | Questions to investigate                                                                                               |
| ------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Configuration and rules        | [Ruler](https://github.com/intellectronica/ruler), [ai-config-sync-manager](https://github.com/slash9494/ai-config-sync-manager), [agent-rules-sync](https://github.com/dhruv-anand-aintech/agent-rules-sync), [ai-rules-sync](https://github.com/lbb00/ai-rules-sync) | Is the authority global or project-local? How are conflicts, external edits and credentials handled?                   |
| Skill distribution             | [skills](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills), [manage-skills](https://github.com/Getty/manage-skills)                                                                                                                                                               | Can existing bundles and their assets be reused without adding another installer?                                      |
| MCP management and aggregation | [mcp-fleet](https://github.com/AZERDSQ131/mcpm), [1MCP](https://github.com/1mcp-app/agent)                                                                                                                                                                             | Should clients receive separate launch definitions or one proxy endpoint? What happens when that proxy is unavailable? |
| Agent handoff                  | [context-relay](https://github.com/krika2810/context-relay), [handoff](https://github.com/zaki2993/handoff)                                                                                                                                                            | How can explicit task notes complement, rather than depend on, transcript extraction?                                  |
| Memory                         | Basic Memory, Memorix, mcp-memory-service, [shared-agent-memory](https://github.com/dan-calin/shared-agent-memory)                                                                                                                                                     | Which interchange formats preserve source identity, atomic knowledge and relationships?                                |
| Conversation search            | [claude-history](https://github.com/raine/claude-history)                                                                                                                                                                                                              | Can existing parsers be reused before building a separate archive index?                                               |

These are research leads. The table does not assert that a project currently supports or lacks a feature.

## Product decisions

1. Reuse local skill bundles and established instruction files. Do not compete with every package installer.
2. Keep MCP credentials in the private Hub environment and refer to variables from the canonical registry.
3. Treat the Hub as authoritative after import. Surface later client differences for a reviewed decision instead of choosing the newest file automatically.
4. Keep project handoff notes explicit: PROJECT.md for durable context and NOW.md for current work. Initialization must not invent architecture or completed checks.
5. Use one memory service for CLI, UI and optional MCP access. Import supported native Markdown without relocating its source. Treat structured graph interchange as separate work.
6. Make the first useful result easy to reach through quick setup, while retaining individual commands for detailed review.

## Risks and open questions

Client formats and hook APIs can change. Adapter fixtures and a real working trial remain necessary. Native client features may reduce the need for a separate Hub; the product must remain useful through clear ownership, safe synchronization and a coherent workflow.

Popularity counts and a few forum threads do not establish product demand. The original research had gaps: inaccessible Reddit discussions, incomplete reviews of several memory systems, unverified third-party popularity figures and no systematic package-download analysis. Those gaps remain research tasks, not release evidence.

Archived-session ingestion, cross-machine configuration policy and structured memory interchange should be driven by concrete user cases and their recovery boundaries. See [Use cases and demand](usecases-and-demand.md) for the original problem categories and [Design](DESIGN.md) for implemented versus planned behavior.

# Use cases and demand: research context

This English editorial summary preserves the problem categories from the original planning notes. Linked discussions are historical research leads; their contents and activity were not revalidated during the quick-start update. This page does not advertise unsupported Agent Hub features or claim that market demand has been established.

## Repeated MCP configuration

A user may configure the same tool in several AI clients, each with a different configuration file and syntax. Updating credentials or arguments separately creates drift.

Agent Hub collects supported existing definitions and delivers reviewed launcher configurations. Quick setup combines those steps. An existing Hub entry remains authoritative; later client edits require a visible decision.

Research lead: [MCPHub: managing MCP servers across AI tools](https://ai.rundatarun.io/practical-applications/mcphub-managing-mcp-servers-across-ai-tools).

## Shared instructions that drift

Teams and individuals may copy the same rules into AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and client-specific files. Copies can diverge intentionally or accidentally.

Hub delivers existing shared rules through owned blocks while preserving personal text. It does not decide that every instruction found in a client should become a global rule.

Research lead: [agentmeld](https://github.com/moneytool/agentmeld).

## Skills copied across projects and clients

Repeated copies make it hard to know which procedure and asset bundle is current. Hub can import complete local bundles and link client roots to the canonical copies. It preserves conflicts and shared-path protections. It does not execute skill scripts during collection or act as a remote package installer.

Research leads: [manage-skills](https://github.com/Getty/manage-skills), [skills](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills).

## Team distribution and reproducibility

Company-managed skill catalogs, pinned dependencies and repeatable setup are related needs. They also introduce questions about trust, updates, source ownership and supply-chain policy.

Agent Hub's current contract is local collection and guarded delivery. Quick does not publish a team registry, configure a cloud remote or install a cross-machine synchronization service.

Research leads: [Ask HN: how do you manage skills files?](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49589914), [NAV tooling](https://ki-utvikling.nav.no/verktoy), [Microsoft APM](https://github.com/microsoft/apm).

## Project knowledge across sessions

Switching clients should not require reconstructing every useful fact or task decision. Hub keeps project knowledge in one scoped collection and handoff files in the repository. Enabled hooks provide project context and request evidenced learning from the active model.

This does not guarantee model compliance, move every native store, ingest old conversations, or silently refresh an existing conversation's context. Standalone Memory MCP access is configured separately for a fixed workspace.

## Predictable changes and recovery

A useful synchronization tool must explain what it reads and writes, preserve unrelated settings, reject stale inputs, and support recovery. Quick shows workflow scope and per-stage outcomes. Individual planners retain their guarded writes and backups; reset returns to the first recorded baseline.

The whole workflow is staged rather than one transaction. A later conflict can leave earlier stages completed. Real client validation remains necessary after restarting clients and handling their trust prompts.

## Alternatives considered

The original notes considered package managers, configuration tools, skill distribution utilities and memory systems. Examples included [APM](https://github.com/microsoft/apm), [agentctl](https://github.com/iheanyi/agentctl), [agentmeld](https://github.com/moneytool/agentmeld), [manage-skills](https://github.com/Getty/manage-skills), and [capshelf](https://github.com/genged/capshelf).

These tools are research references, not a current comparison of supported features. A future comparison should verify capabilities directly and date its evidence.

## What still needs user evidence

A successful automated test does not establish that a workflow saves time or produces useful memory. The next evidence is a real two-client working trial: create a Hub, retrieve a fact in another client, review a native-note conflict, inspect what the model actually saved, and reset a disposable setup.

Use [Quick start](QUICKSTART.md) for the short first-run route and [Working guide](WORKING_GUIDE.md) for detailed scenarios. Keep intentional failure cases inside the isolated laboratory.

questions.question: Does it move a running agent session?
questions.answer: No. Live processes, hidden context and native permissions remain with the original client. This starts a new conversation with reviewed reference material.

questions.question: Will it include the whole conversation?
questions.answer: No. The compact packet uses bounded text excerpts and reports omissions. Tool output and runtime records remain in the full archive. Inspect the source when more detail is needed.

mcp.description: Keep a selected MCP definition in one local Hub. Review imports and delivery to Claude Code, Codex and DeepSeek Harness while preserving unrelated settings.
mcp.heading: One MCP definition. The clients you choose.
mcp.lead: Stop maintaining the same server definition in several client configs. Collect the copy you trust into Hub, then review its delivery to Claude Code, Codex or DeepSeek Harness.
mcp.note: Reviewed changes, per-server choices and recorded recovery. Client permissions still apply.

benefits.title: Compare before replacing
benefits.body: A matching server name does not prove its credentials or arguments match. Inspect differences and choose the intended source.

benefits.title: Keep unrelated settings
benefits.body: Per-server delivery changes the selected entry. Existing Hub launchers are recognized instead of appearing as false configuration conflicts.

benefits.title: Test a real connection
benefits.body: Run a separate connection check to discover tools. A matching configuration alone does not prove the backend is available.

steps.title: Inspect the existing copies
steps.body: Open MCP servers in Hub and compare the trusted Hub and client definitions.

steps.title: Review the direction
steps.body: Import a client copy into Hub, or deliver Hub settings to one client. Each action opens its own preview.

steps.title: Apply and verify
steps.body: Apply the reviewed change, restart the affected client and test the connection when ready.

questions.question: Does every client share one running server?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. Hub shares configuration and client-specific launchers. It does not combine provider subscriptions or guarantee a single shared process.

questions.question: What if a client copy is intentionally different?
questions.answer: Keep that client’s settings. Hub does not silently pick a winner for real differences. Recovery is recorded, but later edits can block an unsafe rollback.

benefits.body: Keep references and assets with the skill. Import copies the local bundle instead of extracting only its main text.

benefits.body: Delivery links selected Hub bundles into supported user roots. Unrelated skills and client-owned plugin scopes remain in place.

steps.body: Review supported local skills or add your own local bundle. Resolve different copies with the same name explicitly.

steps.title: Review delivery
steps.body: Check the clients and physical directories affected. Skills and common instructions have separate delivery previews.

steps.body: Restart the affected client and confirm it sees the skill. A link alone does not prove the agent has invoked it.

questions.question: Do shared instructions update like linked skills?
questions.answer: Not in every client. Skill links point at Hub bundles. Copied instruction blocks need another reviewed context sync after the shared rules change.

questions.question: Does this merge every client’s memory?
questions.answer: No. Shared instructions and the existing shared memory index have a specific scope. Project memory and chat capture are separate workflows.

comparison.description: Choosing between Agent Hub and Hansard? Compare your real chat-search, context-handoff and shared-setup tasks, then check the dated detailed comparison.
comparison.heading: Agent Hub or Hansard? Start with your daily work.
comparison.lead: Choose around a task you repeat: finding a decision, continuing it in another client or maintaining shared tools. Our comparison explains where Agent Hub fits and where you should look further.
comparison.note: Written by the Agent Hub project. Detailed comparison checked on 6 November 2026; not an independent benchmark.
comparison.cardBody: Choose around your workflow, supported clients and practical limits.
comparison.imageAlt: Agent Hub local archive with source and update controls
comparison.caption: Agent Hub’s real archive controls with fictional data. This is not a Hansard screenshot.

benefits.title: Can it read your sources?
benefits.body: Agent Hub reads supported local Claude Code, Codex and DeepSeek Harness formats. Check your actual clients and storage before choosing.

benefits.title: Where do you want to work?
benefits.body: Hub keeps active sessions in native clients. Its interface helps inspect saved data, prepare context and review shared settings.

benefits.title: What will save repeat work?
benefits.body: Try a previous answer and one shared setting. A working search result and a useful next conversation matter more than a feature count.

comparison.stepsTitle: Compare using the same small task.

steps.title: Pick a real decision
steps.body: Choose something you remember discussing but cannot locate quickly. Use the same question in each tool.

steps.title: Inspect the evidence
steps.body: Find the original messages, check the project and date, then identify what remains true in the current code.

steps.title: Continue and decide
steps.body: Continue a small task in another client. Keep the workflow that saves you a repeated manual step.

questions.question: Is Agent Hub a drop-in replacement for Hansard?
questions.answer: Do not assume that. Read the detailed comparison and check current source, platform and workflow support. The tools overlap, but their scope is different.

questions.question: Do I need either tool for one client?
questions.answer: Maybe not. If native search and a short project note already work for you, start there. Try a shared hub when those steps become repeated work.
